oil.filterLocation: Bottom passenger side of engine, spin-on (Subaru boxer layout)

transmission.type: Toyota WS ATF (6-speed auto) or 75W GL-4 (6-speed manual)

jackPoints.front: Reinforced pinch weld behind front wheel
jackPoints.rear: Reinforced pinch weld in front of rear wheel

safety: Boxer engine: spark plugs are on SIDES of engine, not top - horizontal access
Subaru-sourced engine uses Subaru oil filter - not standard Toyota filter
RWD with rear differential - service rear diff at 30K miles
Low sports car - use low-profile jack and quality jack stands
Oil filter is horizontal - will drip when removed, have rags ready

stepHints: Use a LOW-PROFILE jack - this car has very low ground clearance, standard floor jacks may not fit
Raise vehicle on jack stands at reinforced pinch welds behind front wheel
17mm drain plug on oil pan - torque to 31 ft-lbs on reinstall
Oil filter is HORIZONTAL on bottom passenger side (Subaru boxer engine layout) - it WILL drip oil when removed, have rags underneath
Use Subaru OE filter 15208AA170 or Toyota SU003-00311 - NOT a standard Toyota filter
Pre-fill new filter with oil and apply thin coat of oil to gasket before installing
Fill 5.4 quarts 0W-20 with filter - pour 5 quarts first, check dipstick, top off
Start engine, idle 2 minutes, check for leaks (especially at horizontal filter), shut off, recheck level
specialTools: Low-profile floor jack
17mm socket (drain plug)
Oil filter wrench (64mm or strap wrench)
commonMistakes: Using a standard Toyota oil filter - this uses a Subaru filter due to the boxer engine
Not having rags ready for the horizontal filter - it will drip when loosened
Standard floor jack won't fit under the car - need a low-profile jack
Over-filling - only 5.4 quarts, not the typical 4.6 for a Toyota 4-cyl

stepHints: Disconnect negative battery terminal before starting. Let engine cool completely - spark plug work on a hot engine risks burns and thread damage
Boxer/flat engine - spark plugs are accessed horizontally from the sides of the engine. Use extensions and universal joints for access
Remove ignition coil packs one at a time (typically 8mm or 10mm bolt). Label or photograph if concerned about order
Use spark plug socket (typically 5/8" or 16mm) with extension to remove old plugs. Inspect old plugs for abnormal wear patterns
Gap new plugs to 0.030-0.035 in using a feeler gauge before installation

Install FK20HBR-S8 (Denso Iridium) by hand first to avoid cross-threading, then torque to 13 ft-lbs. Do NOT apply anti-seize to modern iridium/platinum plugs - they have factory-applied coating that serves this purpose
Reinstall ignition coils and secure with bolts. Reconnect battery and start engine to verify smooth idle
specialTools: Spark plug socket (5/8" or 16mm, with rubber insert)
Socket extensions (6" and 12")
Torque wrench (inch-lb range)
Feeler gauge or gap tool (0.030-0.035 in)
commonMistakes: Using wrong spark plug - this vehicle requires FK20HBR-S8 (Denso Iridium)
Over-torquing spark plugs (spec is 13 ft-lbs) - overtightening can crack the ceramic or strip aluminum head threads
Applying anti-seize to modern iridium/platinum plugs - they have factory-applied coating, adding more can cause inaccurate torque readings
Installing plugs without checking gap - must be set to 0.030-0.035 in

stepHints: NEVER open a hot cooling system - wait until engine is completely cool. Pressurized coolant can cause severe burns
Locate radiator drain petcock at bottom of radiator (usually driver side). Place drain pan underneath and open to drain old coolant. Capacity is 5.6 qt total system
Once drained, close petcock. Fill system with distilled water, run engine to operating temperature with heater on HIGH, then drain again. Repeat until water runs clear
Refill with Toyota Super Long Life Coolant (pink). Do not mix with other coolant types - Toyota pink coolant is specific to Toyota/Lexus
Bleed air from system: look for bleed valve/screw on thermostat housing or upper radiator hose. Fill slowly, squeeze upper hose to work out air pockets
Run engine to operating temperature with heater on HIGH. Check for leaks at all connections. Recheck coolant level after engine cools and top off
specialTools: Drain pan (capacity for 5.6 qt total system)
Funnel with bleed tube (spill-free type recommended)
Distilled water for flushing
commonMistakes: Using wrong coolant type - this vehicle requires Toyota Super Long Life Coolant (pink)
Mixing different coolant types - can cause gel formation, corrosion, or overheating
Not bleeding air from system - trapped air causes hot spots, overheating, and inaccurate temp gauge readings

stepHints: Raise vehicle securely on jack stands. Locate fill plug (usually on side of transmission) and drain plug (bottom)
IMPORTANT: Remove fill plug FIRST before drain plug - if fill plug is seized, you can still drive with old fluid
Remove drain plug and let fluid drain completely into pan
Install drain plug. Fill through fill plug hole with Toyota WS ATF (6-speed auto) or 75W GL-4 (6-speed manual) using a pump until fluid seeps from fill hole
Total capacity: 3.2 qt (auto), 2.1 qt (manual). Install fill plug once fluid reaches the fill hole level
specialTools: Drain pan
Fluid pump or funnel with long neck
Fluid transfer pump (to fill through side plug)
commonMistakes: Using wrong fluid type - this vehicle requires Toyota WS ATF (6-speed auto) or 75W GL-4 (6-speed manual)
Overfilling transmission - too much fluid causes foaming, overheating, and erratic shifting

stepHints: Raise vehicle securely on jack stands. Locate differential fill and drain plugs
Remove FILL plug first before drain plug - if fill plug is seized, you can still drive with old fluid
REAR differential: drain old fluid, then fill with 75W-90 GL-5 Synthetic - capacity 1.3 qt
Install fill plug once fluid reaches the fill hole level. Check for leaks after test drive
specialTools: Drain pan
Fluid transfer pump (for fill plug)
Ratchet and socket set
commonMistakes: Mixing gear oil weights or types between front and rear differentials - they may require different specifications
Forgetting to remove fill plug first - if seized, you cannot refill the differential

stepHints: SAFETY: Brake fluid is corrosive to paint - immediately wipe any spills. Work in a well-ventilated area
This vehicle requires DOT 3 or DOT 4 brake fluid. Do NOT mix DOT types (especially DOT 5 silicone with DOT 3/4 glycol-based)
Open master cylinder reservoir (under hood, driver side) and top off with fresh DOT 3 or DOT 4. Keep reservoir topped during bleeding
Bleed brakes starting from the wheel FARTHEST from the master cylinder (typically: RR → LR → RF → LF)

At each wheel: attach clear hose to bleeder valve into catch bottle. Have helper pump brake pedal 3x, hold on last pump. Open bleeder briefly until fluid flows, close, then release pedal. Repeat until no bubbles appear
Wheel removal: use 17mm socket for lug nuts. Torque to 89 ft-lbs when reinstalling
After bleeding all 4 corners: pump brake pedal several times to build pressure. Pedal should feel firm - if spongy, re-bleed
specialTools: Brake bleeder wrench (8mm or 10mm, vehicle-specific)
Clear vinyl hose and catch bottle
Fresh DOT 3 or DOT 4 brake fluid (1 quart minimum)
Helper for two-person bleed method (or one-person bleeder kit)
17mm socket and breaker bar (wheel removal)
commonMistakes: Using wrong DOT rating - this vehicle requires DOT 3 or DOT 4
Letting master cylinder reservoir run dry during bleeding - introduces air into system
Not bleeding in correct order (farthest to nearest from master cylinder)
Using old/opened brake fluid - brake fluid absorbs moisture from air rapidly once opened

stepHints: Loosen lug nuts (17mm socket) while wheel is on ground, then raise vehicle and remove wheel
Inspect brake pads through caliper inspection window or by removing caliper. Minimum pad thickness is typically 3mm (1/8") - replace if at or below this
Check brake rotor surface for scoring, grooves, or heat spots (blue discoloration). Measure rotor thickness with micrometer - compare to minimum thickness stamped on rotor
Inspect caliper for leaks, damaged dust boots, and sticky slide pins. Slide pins should move freely
Check brake hoses for cracks, bulging, or leaks
Reinstall wheel and torque lug nuts to 89 ft-lbs in a star/cross pattern. Re-torque after 50-100 miles
specialTools: 17mm socket and breaker bar
Jack and jack stands
Brake pad thickness gauge or micrometer
Flashlight for visual inspection
commonMistakes: Not torquing lug nuts to spec (89 ft-lbs) - under-torque causes wheel loosening, over-torque warps rotors
Ignoring brake fluid level - low fluid often indicates worn pads (fluid fills caliper space as pads wear)
Only checking one corner - brake wear can vary significantly between axles and sides

stepHints: Loosen all lug nuts (17mm socket) while wheels are on ground, then raise vehicle
RWD rotation pattern: Rear tires move straight to front. Front tires cross to opposite rear positions (X-pattern for front tires)
If tires are DIRECTIONAL (arrow on sidewall), they can only be rotated front-to-rear on the same side - never crossed
Check tire pressures and adjust all tires to door placard specification after rotation
Torque all lug nuts to 89 ft-lbs in a star/cross pattern. Re-torque after 50-100 miles of driving
specialTools: 17mm socket and breaker bar
Floor jack and 4 jack stands (or lift)
Torque wrench
Tire pressure gauge
commonMistakes: Not torquing lug nuts to spec (89 ft-lbs)
Rotating directional tires to opposite sides (check for directional arrow on sidewall)
Forgetting to adjust tire pressures after rotation - front and rear specs may differ
Not re-torquing lug nuts/bolts after 50-100 miles

stepHints: Open the hood and locate the air filter box - it is a large plastic housing connected to the intake tube, typically on one side of the engine bay
Release the metal clips (usually 2-4) on the air box lid. Japanese/Korean vehicles typically use simple spring clips that flip open by hand
Lift the lid and remove the old air filter. Note the orientation (airflow direction arrow) for installing the new one
Inspect the air box interior for debris, leaves, or rodent nesting material. Wipe clean if needed
Install the new air filter with the airflow arrow pointing toward the engine (downstream). Ensure it seats flat with no gaps around the edges
Close the air box lid and secure all clips/fasteners. Ensure a tight seal - any air leak bypasses the filter
specialTools: No tools required for most vehicles (hand-release clips)
commonMistakes: Installing filter upside down or backwards - check airflow direction arrow
Not seating filter fully in the air box - gaps allow unfiltered air into engine
Not closing all clips/fasteners on air box lid - causes unmetered air leak and possible check engine light

stepHints: The cabin air filter is accessed behind the glove box
Open the glove box and empty its contents. Squeeze the sides of the glove box inward to release the stop tabs, then lower it fully to reveal the filter housing
On Toyota/Lexus: the damper arm on the right side of the glove box unhooks easily - squeeze the clip to detach
Open the cabin filter housing cover (usually 1-2 tabs). Slide out the old filter, noting the airflow direction arrow
Install the new cabin filter with the airflow direction arrow pointing downward (toward the floor). Ensure it slides in fully and seats flat
Close the filter housing cover, raise the glove box back into position, and re-engage the stop tabs by pushing the sides inward
specialTools: No special tools required for most vehicles
commonMistakes: Installing filter with airflow arrow pointing the wrong direction - check arrow before removing old filter
Forgetting to reinstall glove box stop tabs (glove box hangs open and dumps contents)
Not replacing cabin filter often enough - a clogged filter reduces HVAC airflow and can cause musty odor

stepHints: Before starting: take a photo of the belt routing or find the belt routing diagram (usually on a sticker in the engine bay or in the owner's manual). This is CRITICAL for reinstallation

Locate the automatic belt tensioner - it is spring-loaded with a smooth (unpainted) idler pulley. Use a 15mm wrench, 3/8" square drive ratchet, or vehicle-specific tensioner tool to rotate the tensioner and release belt tension
Slip the old belt off while holding the tensioner. Inspect all pulleys for smooth spinning and wobble - replace any noisy or rough bearings now while the belt is off
Route the new belt according to the diagram, leaving one pulley for last (usually the tensioner idler or alternator). Rotate tensioner, slip belt onto final pulley, and slowly release tensioner
Verify the belt is properly seated in ALL pulley grooves - a misaligned belt will be thrown off immediately. Start engine briefly to confirm belt tracks correctly
specialTools: Serpentine belt tool or 15mm wrench or 3/8" square drive ratchet (for tensioner)
Flashlight (to inspect belt routing and pulley condition)
commonMistakes: Not photographing/documenting belt routing before removal - reinstallation without the diagram is very difficult
Belt not fully seated in a pulley groove - causes squealing, belt damage, or belt being thrown off
Not inspecting idler and tensioner pulleys while belt is off - a failing bearing will destroy the new belt quickly
Releasing tensioner too quickly - let it return slowly to avoid damaging the new belt

stepHints: Open the hood and locate the battery (typically on one side of the engine bay)
SAFETY: Remove any metal jewelry before working on the battery. A wrench bridging positive to ground can cause severe burns or fire
Disconnect the NEGATIVE (-) terminal first (usually 10mm bolt). Move the cable aside so it cannot accidentally contact the terminal
Disconnect the POSITIVE (+) terminal next
Remove the battery hold-down clamp or bracket (typically 10mm, 12mm, or 13mm bolt). Lift the battery out - batteries are heavy (30-50 lbs for cars, 50-75 lbs for trucks)
Clean the battery tray and terminal connectors with baking soda/water solution if there is corrosion. Dry thoroughly
Set new battery in tray and secure hold-down clamp. Connect POSITIVE (+) terminal first, then NEGATIVE (-) last
Apply battery terminal protectant spray or thin layer of dielectric grease to terminals to prevent future corrosion
After connecting: you may need to reset clock, radio presets, and power windows. Some vehicles require an idle relearn procedure - let engine idle for 10 minutes
specialTools: 10mm wrench or socket (terminal bolts)
10mm, 12mm, or 13mm socket (hold-down clamp)
Wire brush or battery terminal cleaner
Memory saver tool (optional - preserves radio, clock, ECU settings during battery swap)
commonMistakes: Disconnecting positive terminal first - always disconnect NEGATIVE first to prevent short circuits
Connecting negative terminal first during installation - always connect POSITIVE first
Not securing hold-down clamp - an unsecured battery can shift and short against the hood
Not cleaning corroded terminals - corrosion on terminals causes voltage drops and starting problems

stepHints: Check your owner's manual or measure your current wiper blades for the correct sizes. Driver and passenger sides are often DIFFERENT lengths
Lift the wiper arm away from the windshield until it locks in the upright position. Place a folded towel on the windshield under the arm in case it snaps back
Press the release tab on the wiper blade where it connects to the arm. Slide the old blade off the hook (most modern vehicles use a J-hook or push-button adapter)
Attach the new blade by sliding it onto the wiper arm hook until it clicks into place. Gently lower the arm back to the windshield and verify it sits flat
Repeat for the other side. Test both wipers with washer fluid to verify proper sweep and no streaking
specialTools: No tools required - wiper blades are a tool-free replacement on most vehicles
commonMistakes: Buying wrong blade size - driver and passenger sides are usually different lengths
Letting wiper arm snap back against windshield without a blade on it - can crack the glass
Not testing new blades with washer fluid - streaking indicates incorrect installation or defective blade
Buying wrong adapter type - verify J-hook, push-button, pin, or bayonet style before purchasing

stepHints: Wheel alignment requires specialized equipment (alignment rack with laser/camera sensors) and should be performed by a qualified shop
Signs you need alignment: vehicle pulls to one side, steering wheel is off-center, uneven tire wear patterns
Before alignment: ensure tire pressures are at specification, suspension components are not worn, and ride height is stock (or inform shop of modifications)
After alignment: the shop should provide a printout showing before/after measurements for camber, caster, and toe. Keep this for your records
Typical cost: $80-150 for a 4-wheel alignment. Get alignment checked after any suspension work, hitting a major pothole, or if tire wear appears uneven
specialTools: Professional alignment rack (shop service only)
commonMistakes: Skipping alignment after suspension work or tire replacement - misalignment causes rapid uneven tire wear
Getting alignment with worn suspension components (ball joints, tie rods, bushings) - alignment will not hold
Not checking tire pressures before alignment - incorrect pressures throw off alignment readings

stepHints: Most modern gasoline vehicles (2006+) have the fuel filter integrated into the fuel pump assembly INSIDE the fuel tank. This is not a routine owner-serviceable item
If your vehicle has an external inline fuel filter (typically older vehicles or some trucks), it is usually located along the fuel line under the vehicle or in the engine bay
Fuel filter replacement involves working with pressurized fuel - consider having a professional handle this service
If fuel delivery issues are suspected (sputtering at high RPM, hard starting, loss of power), have the fuel system professionally diagnosed before assuming the filter is clogged
specialTools: Professional service recommended for most modern vehicles
commonMistakes: Trying to locate an external fuel filter on a vehicle with an in-tank integrated filter/pump assembly
Not relieving fuel system pressure before disconnecting fuel lines

stepHints: Most modern vehicles use Electric Power Steering (EPS) which has NO power steering fluid to change
If your steering feels stiff or makes noise, it is likely an EPS motor or sensor issue - not a fluid problem
Consult your owner's manual to confirm whether your vehicle has hydraulic or electric power steering
commonMistakes: Looking for a power steering fluid reservoir on a vehicle with EPS - there is no fluid to check or change
Attempting to add fluid to a system that does not use hydraulic fluid

stepHints: This engine most likely uses a timing CHAIN, not a timing belt. Timing chains are designed to last the life of the engine under normal conditions
Timing chain replacement is NOT a routine maintenance item - it is only needed if the chain stretches (causes rattling noise at startup or timing-related codes)
If timing chain replacement is needed, it is a major engine service requiring professional disassembly - not a DIY job for most owners
Keep up with oil changes - proper lubrication is critical for timing chain longevity. Skipped oil changes are the #1 cause of premature chain wear
specialTools: Professional service required if chain replacement is needed
commonMistakes: Replacing a timing chain unnecessarily - chains rarely need replacement if oil changes are maintained
Ignoring a rattling noise at cold startup - this can indicate chain stretch and should be inspected before it jumps timing

Unscrew plastic filter housing cap by hand or with a 64mm cap wrench, pull out old element
Replace O-ring on housing cap, install new filter element, hand-tighten cap
Fill 4.8 quarts 0W-20 synthetic oil - pour 4.5 first, check dipstick, top off
Start engine, idle 2 minutes, check for leaks, shut off, wait 5 minutes, recheck
specialTools: 14mm socket (drain plug)
64mm oil filter cap wrench (optional, can hand-tighten)
commonMistakes: Using 5W-30 instead of 0W-20 - Toyota requires 0W-20
Over-torquing the plastic oil drain plug/filter housing
Forgetting to replace crush washer on drain plug

Not bleeding in correct order (farthest to nearest from master cylinder)
Using old/opened brake fluid - brake fluid absorbs moisture from air rapidly once opened

stepHints: Loosen lug nuts (19mm socket) while wheel is on ground, then raise vehicle and remove wheel
Inspect brake pads through caliper inspection window or by removing caliper. Minimum pad thickness is typically 3mm (1/8") - replace if at or below this
Check brake rotor surface for scoring, grooves, or heat spots (blue discoloration). Measure rotor thickness with micrometer - compare to minimum thickness stamped on rotor
Inspect caliper for leaks, damaged dust boots, and sticky slide pins. Slide pins should move freely
Check brake hoses for cracks, bulging, or leaks
Reinstall wheel and torque lug nuts to 80 ft-lbs in a star/cross pattern. Re-torque after 50-100 miles
specialTools: 19mm socket and breaker bar
Jack and jack stands
Brake pad thickness gauge or micrometer
Flashlight for visual inspection
commonMistakes: Not torquing lug nuts to spec (80 ft-lbs) - under-torque causes wheel loosening, over-torque warps rotors
Ignoring brake fluid level - low fluid often indicates worn pads (fluid fills caliper space as pads wear)
Only checking one corner - brake wear can vary significantly between axles and sides

stepHints: Loosen all lug nuts (19mm socket) while wheels are on ground, then raise vehicle
RWD rotation pattern: Rear tires move straight to front. Front tires cross to opposite rear positions (X-pattern for front tires)
If tires are DIRECTIONAL (arrow on sidewall), they can only be rotated front-to-rear on the same side - never crossed
Check tire pressures and adjust all tires to door placard specification after rotation
Torque all lug nuts to 80 ft-lbs in a star/cross pattern. Re-torque after 50-100 miles of driving
specialTools: 19mm socket and breaker bar
Floor jack and 4 jack stands (or lift)
Torque wrench
Tire pressure gauge
commonMistakes: Not torquing lug nuts to spec (80 ft-lbs)
Rotating directional tires to opposite sides (check for directional arrow on sidewall)
Forgetting to adjust tire pressures after rotation - front and rear specs may differ
Not re-torquing lug nuts/bolts after 50-100 miles

stepHints: Open the hood and locate the air filter box - it is a large plastic housing connected to the intake tube, typically on one side of the engine bay
Release the metal clips (usually 2-4) on the air box lid. Japanese/Korean vehicles typically use simple spring clips that flip open by hand
Lift the lid and remove the old air filter. Note the orientation (airflow direction arrow) for installing the new one
Inspect the air box interior for debris, leaves, or rodent nesting material. Wipe clean if needed
Install the new air filter with the airflow arrow pointing toward the engine (downstream). Ensure it seats flat with no gaps around the edges
Close the air box lid and secure all clips/fasteners. Ensure a tight seal - any air leak bypasses the filter
specialTools: No tools required for most vehicles (hand-release clips)
commonMistakes: Installing filter upside down or backwards - check airflow direction arrow
Not seating filter fully in the air box - gaps allow unfiltered air into engine
Not closing all clips/fasteners on air box lid - causes unmetered air leak and possible check engine light
Going too long between changes in dusty conditions - trucks and diesels should change filter more frequently in dusty environments

stepHints: The cabin air filter is accessed behind the glove box
Open the glove box and empty its contents. Squeeze the sides of the glove box inward to release the stop tabs, then lower it fully to reveal the filter housing
On Honda/Acura: remove the glove box damper arm (right side) by pushing the pin inward, then squeeze sides and lower
Open the cabin filter housing cover (usually 1-2 tabs). Slide out the old filter, noting the airflow direction arrow
Install the new cabin filter with the airflow direction arrow pointing downward (toward the floor). Ensure it slides in fully and seats flat
Close the filter housing cover, raise the glove box back into position, and re-engage the stop tabs by pushing the sides inward
specialTools: No special tools required for most vehicles
commonMistakes: Installing filter with airflow arrow pointing the wrong direction - check arrow before removing old filter
Forgetting to reinstall glove box stop tabs (glove box hangs open and dumps contents)
Not replacing cabin filter often enough - a clogged filter reduces HVAC airflow and can cause musty odor

stepHints: Before starting: take a photo of the belt routing or find the belt routing diagram (usually on a sticker in the engine bay or in the owner's manual). This is CRITICAL for reinstallation

Locate the automatic belt tensioner - it is spring-loaded with a smooth (unpainted) idler pulley. Use a 15mm wrench, 3/8" square drive ratchet, or vehicle-specific tensioner tool to rotate the tensioner and release belt tension

On V6/V8 engines, the belt route is complex and wraps around many pulleys (alternator, A/C, power steering, water pump, idler, tensioner). Work from the top of the engine and reference your routing diagram
Slip the old belt off while holding the tensioner. Inspect all pulleys for smooth spinning and wobble - replace any noisy or rough bearings now while the belt is off
Route the new belt according to the diagram, leaving one pulley for last (usually the tensioner idler or alternator). Rotate tensioner, slip belt onto final pulley, and slowly release tensioner
Verify the belt is properly seated in ALL pulley grooves - a misaligned belt will be thrown off immediately. Start engine briefly to confirm belt tracks correctly

Flashlight (to inspect belt routing and pulley condition)

Belt not fully seated in a pulley groove - causes squealing, belt damage, or belt being thrown off
Not inspecting idler and tensioner pulleys while belt is off - a failing bearing will destroy the new belt quickly
Releasing tensioner too quickly - let it return slowly to avoid damaging the new belt

stepHints: Open the hood and locate the battery (typically on one side of the engine bay)

Disconnect the POSITIVE (+) terminal next
Remove the battery hold-down clamp or bracket (typically 10mm, 12mm, or 13mm bolt). Lift the battery out - batteries are heavy (30-50 lbs for cars, 50-75 lbs for trucks)
Clean the battery tray and terminal connectors with baking soda/water solution if there is corrosion. Dry thoroughly
Set new battery in tray and secure hold-down clamp. Connect POSITIVE (+) terminal first, then NEGATIVE (-) last
Apply battery terminal protectant spray or thin layer of dielectric grease to terminals to prevent future corrosion

Not securing hold-down clamp - an unsecured battery can shift and short against the hood
Not cleaning corroded terminals - corrosion on terminals causes voltage drops and starting problems

stepHints: Check your owner's manual or measure your current wiper blades for the correct sizes. Driver and passenger sides are often DIFFERENT lengths

Attach the new blade by sliding it onto the wiper arm hook until it clicks into place. Gently lower the arm back to the windshield and verify it sits flat
Repeat for the other side. Test both wipers with washer fluid to verify proper sweep and no streaking

commonMistakes: Buying wrong blade size - driver and passenger sides are usually different lengths
Letting wiper arm snap back against windshield without a blade on it - can crack the glass
Not testing new blades with washer fluid - streaking indicates incorrect installation or defective blade
Buying wrong adapter type - verify J-hook, push-button, pin, or bayonet style before purchasing

specialTools: Professional alignment rack (shop service only)
commonMistakes: Skipping alignment after suspension work or tire replacement - misalignment causes rapid uneven tire wear

If your vehicle has an external inline fuel filter (typically older vehicles or some trucks), it is usually located along the fuel line under the vehicle or in the engine bay

Consult your owner's manual to confirm whether your vehicle has hydraulic or electric power steering
commonMistakes: Looking for a power steering fluid reservoir on a vehicle with EPS - there is no fluid to check or change

stepHints: Timing belt replacement is a MAJOR service - typically recommended every 60,000-105,000 miles depending on the engine
This is NOT a DIY job for most owners - it requires significant engine disassembly, specialized tools, and precise timing alignment
IMPORTANT: Many timing belt engines are "interference" designs - if the belt breaks, valves contact pistons causing catastrophic engine damage
When replacing the timing belt, also replace the water pump, tensioner, and idler pulleys (they share the same service life)
Have a qualified mechanic perform this service. Typical cost is $500-1,200 depending on the vehicle
Verify your engine's replacement interval in the owner's manual - do NOT exceed the recommended mileage
specialTools: Professional service strongly recommended
commonMistakes: Exceeding the timing belt replacement interval - a snapped belt on an interference engine destroys the engine
Replacing only the belt and not the water pump/tensioner/idler - these components share the same service life and failing any one of them ruins the new belt
Attempting as a DIY project without proper training - incorrect timing will cause the engine to run poorly or not at all

stepHints: Raise vehicle on jack stands or ramps - frame rail behind front wheel is the jack point

stepHints: Disconnect negative battery terminal before starting. Let engine cool completely - spark plug work on a hot engine risks burns and thread damage
This is a V6 engine with 6 plugs. Front bank (3 plugs) is easily accessible. Rear bank may require removing intake manifold or reaching from behind engine
Remove ignition coil packs one at a time (typically 8mm or 10mm bolt). Label or photograph if concerned about order

Gap new plugs to 0.028-0.032 in (EB), 0.052 in (5.0L) using a feeler gauge before installation

Install SP-534 (Motorcraft, 3.5L EB), SP-542A (5.0L) by hand first to avoid cross-threading, then torque to 9 ft-lbs (EB - DO NOT overtorque, plugs can break). Do NOT apply anti-seize to modern iridium/platinum plugs - they have factory-applied coating that serves this purpose
Reinstall ignition coils and secure with bolts. Reconnect battery and start engine to verify smooth idle
specialTools: Spark plug socket (5/8" or 16mm, with rubber insert)

commonMistakes: Using wrong spark plug - this vehicle requires SP-534 (Motorcraft, 3.5L EB), SP-542A (5.0L)

Locate radiator drain petcock at bottom of radiator (usually driver side). Place drain pan underneath and open to drain old coolant. Capacity is 13.1 qt total system (3.5L EcoBoost)
Once drained, close petcock. Fill system with distilled water, run engine to operating temperature with heater on HIGH, then drain again. Repeat until water runs clear
Refill with Motorcraft Orange Coolant (VC-3DIL-B). Use 50/50 mix with distilled water unless using pre-mixed
Bleed air from system: look for bleed valve/screw on thermostat housing or upper radiator hose. Fill slowly, squeeze upper hose to work out air pockets
Run engine to operating temperature with heater on HIGH. Check for leaks at all connections. Recheck coolant level after engine cools and top off
specialTools: Drain pan (capacity for 13.1 qt total system (3.5L EcoBoost))
Funnel with bleed tube (spill-free type recommended)
Distilled water for flushing
commonMistakes: Using wrong coolant type - this vehicle requires Motorcraft Orange Coolant (VC-3DIL-B)
Mixing different coolant types - can cause gel formation, corrosion, or overheating

stepHints: Warm transmission to operating temperature by driving 10-15 minutes before draining

specialTools: Drain pan
Fluid pump or funnel with long neck
commonMistakes: Using wrong fluid type - this vehicle requires Mercon ULV ATF (10R80 10-speed)

Checking fluid level with engine off or transmission not in Park - gives inaccurate reading

Fluid transfer pump (for fill plug)
Ratchet and socket set

Refill with 5.7 qt (2.3L), 6.0 qt (3.0L) with filter of 5W-30 Full Synthetic

Gap new plugs to 0.030 in using a feeler gauge before installation

Installing plugs without checking gap - must be set to 0.030 in

Not bleeding air from system - trapped air causes hot spots, overheating, and inaccurate temp gauge readings

Check fluid level with engine running, transmission in Park, at operating temperature. Level should be in the crosshatch area on dipstick

stepHints: SAFETY: Brake fluid is corrosive to paint - immediately wipe any spills. Work in a well-ventilated area
This vehicle requires DOT 4 brake fluid. Do NOT mix DOT types (especially DOT 5 silicone with DOT 3/4 glycol-based)
Open master cylinder reservoir (under hood, driver side) and top off with fresh DOT 4. Keep reservoir topped during bleeding
Bleed brakes starting from the wheel FARTHEST from the master cylinder (typically: RR → LR → RF → LF)

At each wheel: attach clear hose to bleeder valve into catch bottle. Have helper pump brake pedal 3x, hold on last pump. Open bleeder briefly until fluid flows, close, then release pedal. Repeat until no bubbles appear
Wheel removal: use 21mm socket for lug nuts. Torque to 150 ft-lbs when reinstalling
After bleeding all 4 corners: pump brake pedal several times to build pressure. Pedal should feel firm - if spongy, re-bleed

Helper for two-person bleed method (or one-person bleeder kit)
21mm socket and breaker bar (wheel removal)
commonMistakes: Using wrong DOT rating - this vehicle requires DOT 4
Letting master cylinder reservoir run dry during bleeding - introduces air into system
Not bleeding in correct order (farthest to nearest from master cylinder)
Using old/opened brake fluid - brake fluid absorbs moisture from air rapidly once opened

stepHints: Loosen lug nuts (21mm socket) while wheel is on ground, then raise vehicle and remove wheel
Inspect brake pads through caliper inspection window or by removing caliper. Minimum pad thickness is typically 3mm (1/8") - replace if at or below this
Check brake rotor surface for scoring, grooves, or heat spots (blue discoloration). Measure rotor thickness with micrometer - compare to minimum thickness stamped on rotor
Inspect caliper for leaks, damaged dust boots, and sticky slide pins. Slide pins should move freely
Check brake hoses for cracks, bulging, or leaks
Reinstall wheel and torque lug nuts to 150 ft-lbs in a star/cross pattern. Re-torque after 50-100 miles
specialTools: 21mm socket and breaker bar
Jack and jack stands
Brake pad thickness gauge or micrometer
Flashlight for visual inspection
commonMistakes: Not torquing lug nuts to spec (150 ft-lbs) - under-torque causes wheel loosening, over-torque warps rotors
Ignoring brake fluid level - low fluid often indicates worn pads (fluid fills caliper space as pads wear)

stepHints: Loosen all lug nuts (21mm socket) while wheels are on ground, then raise vehicle
FWD rotation pattern: Front tires move straight to rear. Rear tires cross to opposite front positions (X-pattern for rear tires)

Check tire pressures and adjust all tires to door placard specification after rotation
Torque all lug nuts to 150 ft-lbs in a star/cross pattern. Re-torque after 50-100 miles of driving

Torque wrench

Rotating directional tires to opposite sides (check for directional arrow on sidewall)

stepHints: Open the hood and locate the air filter box - it is a large plastic housing connected to the intake tube, typically on one side of the engine bay
Release the clips or fasteners on the air box lid. Most have 2-4 spring clips that unsnap by hand
Lift the lid and remove the old air filter. Note the orientation (airflow direction arrow) for installing the new one
Inspect the air box interior for debris, leaves, or rodent nesting material. Wipe clean if needed
Install the new air filter with the airflow arrow pointing toward the engine (downstream). Ensure it seats flat with no gaps around the edges
Close the air box lid and secure all clips/fasteners. Ensure a tight seal - any air leak bypasses the filter
specialTools: No tools required for most vehicles (hand-release clips)
commonMistakes: Installing filter upside down or backwards - check airflow direction arrow
Not seating filter fully in the air box - gaps allow unfiltered air into engine

stepHints: The cabin air filter is accessed behind the glove box
Open the glove box and empty its contents. Squeeze the sides of the glove box inward to release the stop tabs, then lower it fully to reveal the filter housing
Open the cabin filter housing cover (usually 1-2 tabs). Slide out the old filter, noting the airflow direction arrow
Install the new cabin filter with the airflow direction arrow pointing downward (toward the floor). Ensure it slides in fully and seats flat
Close the filter housing cover, raise the glove box back into position, and re-engage the stop tabs by pushing the sides inward
specialTools: No special tools required for most vehicles
commonMistakes: Installing filter with airflow arrow pointing the wrong direction - check arrow before removing old filter
Forgetting to reinstall glove box stop tabs (glove box hangs open and dumps contents)
Not replacing cabin filter often enough - a clogged filter reduces HVAC airflow and can cause musty odor

stepHints: Before starting: take a photo of the belt routing or find the belt routing diagram (usually on a sticker in the engine bay or in the owner's manual). This is CRITICAL for reinstallation

Locate the automatic belt tensioner - it is spring-loaded with a smooth (unpainted) idler pulley. Use a 15mm wrench, 3/8" square drive ratchet, or vehicle-specific tensioner tool to rotate the tensioner and release belt tension

On V6/V8 engines, the belt route is complex and wraps around many pulleys (alternator, A/C, power steering, water pump, idler, tensioner). Work from the top of the engine and reference your routing diagram
Slip the old belt off while holding the tensioner. Inspect all pulleys for smooth spinning and wobble - replace any noisy or rough bearings now while the belt is off
Route the new belt according to the diagram, leaving one pulley for last (usually the tensioner idler or alternator). Rotate tensioner, slip belt onto final pulley, and slowly release tensioner
Verify the belt is properly seated in ALL pulley grooves - a misaligned belt will be thrown off immediately. Start engine briefly to confirm belt tracks correctly
specialTools: Serpentine belt tool or 15mm wrench or 3/8" square drive ratchet (for tensioner)
Flashlight (to inspect belt routing and pulley condition)
commonMistakes: Not photographing/documenting belt routing before removal - reinstallation without the diagram is very difficult
Belt not fully seated in a pulley groove - causes squealing, belt damage, or belt being thrown off
Not inspecting idler and tensioner pulleys while belt is off - a failing bearing will destroy the new belt quickly
Releasing tensioner too quickly - let it return slowly to avoid damaging the new belt

stepHints: Open the hood and locate the battery (typically on one side of the engine bay)
SAFETY: Remove any metal jewelry before working on the battery. A wrench bridging positive to ground can cause severe burns or fire
Disconnect the NEGATIVE (-) terminal first (usually 10mm bolt). Move the cable aside so it cannot accidentally contact the terminal
Disconnect the POSITIVE (+) terminal next
Remove the battery hold-down clamp or bracket (typically 10mm, 12mm, or 13mm bolt). Lift the battery out - batteries are heavy (30-50 lbs for cars, 50-75 lbs for trucks)
Clean the battery tray and terminal connectors with baking soda/water solution if there is corrosion. Dry thoroughly
Set new battery in tray and secure hold-down clamp. Connect POSITIVE (+) terminal first, then NEGATIVE (-) last
Apply battery terminal protectant spray or thin layer of dielectric grease to terminals to prevent future corrosion
After connecting: you may need to reset clock, radio presets, and power windows. Some vehicles require an idle relearn procedure - let engine idle for 10 minutes
specialTools: 10mm wrench or socket (terminal bolts)
10mm, 12mm, or 13mm socket (hold-down clamp)
Wire brush or battery terminal cleaner
Memory saver tool (optional - preserves radio, clock, ECU settings during battery swap)
commonMistakes: Disconnecting positive terminal first - always disconnect NEGATIVE first to prevent short circuits
Connecting negative terminal first during installation - always connect POSITIVE first
Not securing hold-down clamp - an unsecured battery can shift and short against the hood
Not cleaning corroded terminals - corrosion on terminals causes voltage drops and starting problems

stepHints: Check your owner's manual or measure your current wiper blades for the correct sizes. Driver and passenger sides are often DIFFERENT lengths
Lift the wiper arm away from the windshield until it locks in the upright position. Place a folded towel on the windshield under the arm in case it snaps back
Press the release tab on the wiper blade where it connects to the arm. Slide the old blade off the hook (most modern vehicles use a J-hook or push-button adapter)
Attach the new blade by sliding it onto the wiper arm hook until it clicks into place. Gently lower the arm back to the windshield and verify it sits flat
Repeat for the other side. Test both wipers with washer fluid to verify proper sweep and no streaking
This vehicle may have a REAR wiper blade as well. Check if the rear wiper needs replacement - it often uses a different size and attachment style
specialTools: No tools required - wiper blades are a tool-free replacement on most vehicles
commonMistakes: Buying wrong blade size - driver and passenger sides are usually different lengths
Letting wiper arm snap back against windshield without a blade on it - can crack the glass
Not testing new blades with washer fluid - streaking indicates incorrect installation or defective blade
Buying wrong adapter type - verify J-hook, push-button, pin, or bayonet style before purchasing

stepHints: Wheel alignment requires specialized equipment (alignment rack with laser/camera sensors) and should be performed by a qualified shop
Signs you need alignment: vehicle pulls to one side, steering wheel is off-center, uneven tire wear patterns
Before alignment: ensure tire pressures are at specification, suspension components are not worn, and ride height is stock (or inform shop of modifications)
After alignment: the shop should provide a printout showing before/after measurements for camber, caster, and toe. Keep this for your records

Getting alignment with worn suspension components (ball joints, tie rods, bushings) - alignment will not hold
Not checking tire pressures before alignment - incorrect pressures throw off alignment readings

stepHints: Identify which bulb needs replacement — check all exterior lights with the vehicle running and someone outside to confirm
This vehicle uses LED modules for headlights — these are not user-serviceable bulbs. If an LED headlight fails, the entire module or assembly must be replaced by a dealer or specialist

stepHints: Open the hood and locate the air filter box - it is a large plastic housing connected to the intake tube, typically on one side of the engine bay

Install the new air filter with the airflow arrow pointing toward the engine (downstream). Ensure it seats flat with no gaps around the edges

Install the new cabin filter with the airflow direction arrow pointing downward (toward the floor). Ensure it slides in fully and seats flat

stepHints: Before starting: take a photo of the belt routing or find the belt routing diagram (usually on a sticker in the engine bay or in the owner's manual). This is CRITICAL for reinstallation

Locate the automatic belt tensioner - it is spring-loaded with a smooth (unpainted) idler pulley. Use a 15mm wrench, 3/8" square drive ratchet, or vehicle-specific tensioner tool to rotate the tensioner and release belt tension
Slip the old belt off while holding the tensioner. Inspect all pulleys for smooth spinning and wobble - replace any noisy or rough bearings now while the belt is off
Route the new belt according to the diagram, leaving one pulley for last (usually the tensioner idler or alternator). Rotate tensioner, slip belt onto final pulley, and slowly release tensioner
Verify the belt is properly seated in ALL pulley grooves - a misaligned belt will be thrown off immediately. Start engine briefly to confirm belt tracks correctly

Belt not fully seated in a pulley groove - causes squealing, belt damage, or belt being thrown off
Not inspecting idler and tensioner pulleys while belt is off - a failing bearing will destroy the new belt quickly
Releasing tensioner too quickly - let it return slowly to avoid damaging the new belt

stepHints: Open the hood and locate the battery (typically on one side of the engine bay)
SAFETY: Remove any metal jewelry before working on the battery. A wrench bridging positive to ground can cause severe burns or fire
Disconnect the NEGATIVE (-) terminal first (usually 10mm bolt). Move the cable aside so it cannot accidentally contact the terminal
Disconnect the POSITIVE (+) terminal next
Remove the battery hold-down clamp or bracket (typically 10mm, 12mm, or 13mm bolt). Lift the battery out - batteries are heavy (30-50 lbs for cars, 50-75 lbs for trucks)
Clean the battery tray and terminal connectors with baking soda/water solution if there is corrosion. Dry thoroughly
Set new battery in tray and secure hold-down clamp. Connect POSITIVE (+) terminal first, then NEGATIVE (-) last
Apply battery terminal protectant spray or thin layer of dielectric grease to terminals to prevent future corrosion
After connecting: you may need to reset clock, radio presets, and power windows. Some vehicles require an idle relearn procedure - let engine idle for 10 minutes
specialTools: 10mm wrench or socket (terminal bolts)
10mm, 12mm, or 13mm socket (hold-down clamp)
Wire brush or battery terminal cleaner
Memory saver tool (optional - preserves radio, clock, ECU settings during battery swap)
commonMistakes: Disconnecting positive terminal first - always disconnect NEGATIVE first to prevent short circuits
Connecting negative terminal first during installation - always connect POSITIVE first
Not securing hold-down clamp - an unsecured battery can shift and short against the hood
Not cleaning corroded terminals - corrosion on terminals causes voltage drops and starting problems

stepHints: Check your owner's manual or measure your current wiper blades for the correct sizes. Driver and passenger sides are often DIFFERENT lengths
Lift the wiper arm away from the windshield until it locks in the upright position. Place a folded towel on the windshield under the arm in case it snaps back
Press the release tab on the wiper blade where it connects to the arm. Slide the old blade off the hook (most modern vehicles use a J-hook or push-button adapter)
Attach the new blade by sliding it onto the wiper arm hook until it clicks into place. Gently lower the arm back to the windshield and verify it sits flat
Repeat for the other side. Test both wipers with washer fluid to verify proper sweep and no streaking

commonMistakes: Buying wrong blade size - driver and passenger sides are usually different lengths

Not testing new blades with washer fluid - streaking indicates incorrect installation or defective blade
Buying wrong adapter type - verify J-hook, push-button, pin, or bayonet style before purchasing

stepHints: Wheel alignment requires specialized equipment (alignment rack with laser/camera sensors) and should be performed by a qualified shop

stepHints: Most modern gasoline vehicles (2006+) have the fuel filter integrated into the fuel pump assembly INSIDE the fuel tank. This is not a routine owner-serviceable item

stepHints: This engine most likely uses a timing CHAIN, not a timing belt. Timing chains are designed to last the life of the engine under normal conditions

stepHints: Open the hood and locate the air filter box - it is a large plastic housing connected to the intake tube, typically on one side of the engine bay
Release the clips or fasteners on the air box lid. Most have 2-4 spring clips that unsnap by hand
TURBOCHARGED ENGINE: You may need to disconnect the MAF sensor electrical connector and/or loosen the intake tube clamp before fully removing the air box lid
Lift the lid and remove the old air filter. Note the orientation (airflow direction arrow) for installing the new one
Inspect the air box interior for debris, leaves, or rodent nesting material. Wipe clean if needed
Install the new air filter with the airflow arrow pointing toward the engine (downstream). Ensure it seats flat with no gaps around the edges
Close the air box lid and secure all clips/fasteners. Ensure a tight seal - any air leak bypasses the filter
Reconnect MAF sensor connector and tighten intake tube clamp if disconnected

Install the new cabin filter with the airflow direction arrow pointing downward (toward the floor). Ensure it slides in fully and seats flat
Close the filter housing cover, raise the glove box back into position, and re-engage the stop tabs by pushing the sides inward

stepHints: Before starting: take a photo of the belt routing or find the belt routing diagram (usually on a sticker in the engine bay or in the owner's manual). This is CRITICAL for reinstallation

On V6/V8 engines, the belt route is complex and wraps around many pulleys (alternator, A/C, power steering, water pump, idler, tensioner). Work from the top of the engine and reference your routing diagram
Slip the old belt off while holding the tensioner. Inspect all pulleys for smooth spinning and wobble - replace any noisy or rough bearings now while the belt is off
Route the new belt according to the diagram, leaving one pulley for last (usually the tensioner idler or alternator). Rotate tensioner, slip belt onto final pulley, and slowly release tensioner
Verify the belt is properly seated in ALL pulley grooves - a misaligned belt will be thrown off immediately. Start engine briefly to confirm belt tracks correctly

Flashlight (to inspect belt routing and pulley condition)

stepHints: Open the hood and locate the air filter box - it is a large plastic housing connected to the intake tube, typically on one side of the engine bay

stepHints: Before starting: take a photo of the belt routing or find the belt routing diagram (usually on a sticker in the engine bay or in the owner's manual). This is CRITICAL for reinstallation

Refill with Dex-Cool (orange). IMPORTANT: Dex-Cool must NOT be mixed with traditional green coolant - mixing causes gel formation and clogs
Bleed air from system: look for bleed valve/screw on thermostat housing or upper radiator hose. Fill slowly, squeeze upper hose to work out air pockets
Run engine to operating temperature with heater on HIGH. Check for leaks at all connections. Recheck coolant level after engine cools and top off

Funnel with bleed tube (spill-free type recommended)
Distilled water for flushing

Mixing different coolant types - can cause gel formation, corrosion, or overheating
Not bleeding air from system - trapped air causes hot spots, overheating, and inaccurate temp gauge readings

stepHints: Warm transmission to operating temperature by driving 10-15 minutes before draining
Locate transmission drain plug or pan bolts. Remove and drain fluid into pan. Drain and fill capacity: 5.0 qt drain and fill

Check fluid level with engine running, transmission in Park, at operating temperature. Level should be in the crosshatch area on dipstick
Perform a drain-and-fill (NOT a full flush) to exchange approximately 30-40% of total fluid volume. Repeat at next interval for gradual refresh
specialTools: Drain pan
Fluid pump or funnel with long neck
commonMistakes: Using wrong fluid type - this vehicle requires Dexron HP (9T65 9-speed auto)
Overfilling transmission - too much fluid causes foaming, overheating, and erratic shifting
Checking fluid level with engine off or transmission not in Park - gives inaccurate reading

stepHints: SAFETY: Brake fluid is corrosive to paint - immediately wipe any spills. Work in a well-ventilated area

Bleed brakes starting from the wheel FARTHEST from the master cylinder (typically: RR → LR → RF → LF)

Wheel removal: use 19mm socket for lug nuts. Torque to 100 ft-lbs when reinstalling

Inspect caliper for leaks, damaged dust boots, and sticky slide pins. Slide pins should move freely
Check brake hoses for cracks, bulging, or leaks
Reinstall wheel and torque lug nuts to 100 ft-lbs in a star/cross pattern. Re-torque after 50-100 miles

Jack and jack stands
Brake pad thickness gauge or micrometer
Flashlight for visual inspection

stepHints: Loosen all lug nuts (19mm socket) while wheels are on ground, then raise vehicle

Torque all lug nuts to 100 ft-lbs in a star/cross pattern. Re-torque after 50-100 miles of driving

stepHints: Open the hood and locate the air filter box - it is a large plastic housing connected to the intake tube, typically on one side of the engine bay
Release the clips or fasteners on the air box lid. Most have 2-4 spring clips that unsnap by hand
TURBOCHARGED ENGINE: You may need to disconnect the MAF sensor electrical connector and/or loosen the intake tube clamp before fully removing the air box lid
Lift the lid and remove the old air filter. Note the orientation (airflow direction arrow) for installing the new one
Inspect the air box interior for debris, leaves, or rodent nesting material. Wipe clean if needed
Install the new air filter with the airflow arrow pointing toward the engine (downstream). Ensure it seats flat with no gaps around the edges
Close the air box lid and secure all clips/fasteners. Ensure a tight seal - any air leak bypasses the filter

Open the cabin filter housing cover (usually 1-2 tabs). Slide out the old filter, noting the airflow direction arrow
Install the new cabin filter with the airflow direction arrow pointing downward (toward the floor). Ensure it slides in fully and seats flat

commonMistakes: Installing filter with airflow arrow pointing the wrong direction - check arrow before removing old filter

stepHints: Before starting: take a photo of the belt routing or find the belt routing diagram (usually on a sticker in the engine bay or in the owner's manual). This is CRITICAL for reinstallation

Route the new belt according to the diagram, leaving one pulley for last (usually the tensioner idler or alternator). Rotate tensioner, slip belt onto final pulley, and slowly release tensioner

Releasing tensioner too quickly - let it return slowly to avoid damaging the new belt

stepHints: Wheel alignment requires specialized equipment (alignment rack with laser/camera sensors) and should be performed by a qualified shop

commonMistakes: Skipping alignment after suspension work or tire replacement - misalignment causes rapid uneven tire wear

stepHints: Most modern gasoline vehicles (2006+) have the fuel filter integrated into the fuel pump assembly INSIDE the fuel tank. This is not a routine owner-serviceable item
If your vehicle has an external inline fuel filter (typically older vehicles or some trucks), it is usually located along the fuel line under the vehicle or in the engine bay
Fuel filter replacement involves working with pressurized fuel - consider having a professional handle this service
If fuel delivery issues are suspected (sputtering at high RPM, hard starting, loss of power), have the fuel system professionally diagnosed before assuming the filter is clogged
specialTools: Professional service recommended for most modern vehicles
commonMistakes: Trying to locate an external fuel filter on a vehicle with an in-tank integrated filter/pump assembly
Not relieving fuel system pressure before disconnecting fuel lines

stepHints: Most modern vehicles use Electric Power Steering (EPS) which has NO power steering fluid to change
If your steering feels stiff or makes noise, it is likely an EPS motor or sensor issue - not a fluid problem
Consult your owner's manual to confirm whether your vehicle has hydraulic or electric power steering
commonMistakes: Looking for a power steering fluid reservoir on a vehicle with EPS - there is no fluid to check or change

stepHints: Timing belt replacement is a MAJOR service - typically recommended every 60,000-105,000 miles depending on the engine
This is NOT a DIY job for most owners - it requires significant engine disassembly, specialized tools, and precise timing alignment
IMPORTANT: Many timing belt engines are "interference" designs - if the belt breaks, valves contact pistons causing catastrophic engine damage
When replacing the timing belt, also replace the water pump, tensioner, and idler pulleys (they share the same service life)
Have a qualified mechanic perform this service. Typical cost is $500-1,200 depending on the vehicle
Verify your engine's replacement interval in the owner's manual - do NOT exceed the recommended mileage
specialTools: Professional service strongly recommended
commonMistakes: Exceeding the timing belt replacement interval - a snapped belt on an interference engine destroys the engine
Replacing only the belt and not the water pump/tensioner/idler - these components share the same service life and failing any one of them ruins the new belt
Attempting as a DIY project without proper training - incorrect timing will cause the engine to run poorly or not at all

stepHints: Identify which bulb needs replacement — check all exterior lights with the vehicle running and someone outside to confirm
Low beam bulb: H11. High beam bulb: 9005. Access from behind the headlight housing in the engine bay
Turn the bulb socket counterclockwise to remove it from the housing. Pull the old bulb straight out of the socket

Insert the new bulb into the socket, align the tabs, and twist clockwise to lock into the housing

Turn signal bulbs: Front 7444, Rear 7440. If turn signals flash rapidly (hyperflash), a bulb is burnt out
Reverse light: 921. License plate light: 194. Access through the trunk or hatch interior
After replacement, test all lights: low beam, high beam, turn signals (both sides), brake lights, reverse, fog lights, and running lights
specialTools: Gloves (nitrile or cotton — do not touch halogen bulbs with bare skin)
Flat-head screwdriver or trim removal tool (for accessing some housings)
Flashlight (to see inside the headlight housing area)
commonMistakes: Touching halogen bulb glass with bare fingers — causes premature failure from oil deposits
Forcing the bulb socket — if it does not turn easily, check alignment of the tabs
Not testing all lights after replacement — always verify both sides and all functions
Buying the wrong bulb size — double-check the owner's manual or the old bulb before purchasing
Mixing halogen and LED bulbs without proper resistors — causes hyperflash on turn signals and may trigger warnings

Before alignment: ensure tire pressures are at specification, suspension components are not worn, and ride height is stock (or inform shop of modifications)
After alignment: the shop should provide a printout showing before/after measurements for camber, caster, and toe. Keep this for your records
Typical cost: $80-150 for a 4-wheel alignment. Get alignment checked after any suspension work, hitting a major pothole, or if tire wear appears uneven
specialTools: Professional alignment rack (shop service only)
commonMistakes: Skipping alignment after suspension work or tire replacement - misalignment causes rapid uneven tire wear
Getting alignment with worn suspension components (ball joints, tie rods, bushings) - alignment will not hold
Not checking tire pressures before alignment - incorrect pressures throw off alignment readings

stepHints: Most modern gasoline vehicles (2006+) have the fuel filter integrated into the fuel pump assembly INSIDE the fuel tank. This is not a routine owner-serviceable item
If your vehicle has an external inline fuel filter (typically older vehicles or some trucks), it is usually located along the fuel line under the vehicle or in the engine bay
Fuel filter replacement involves working with pressurized fuel - consider having a professional handle this service
If fuel delivery issues are suspected (sputtering at high RPM, hard starting, loss of power), have the fuel system professionally diagnosed before assuming the filter is clogged
specialTools: Professional service recommended for most modern vehicles
commonMistakes: Trying to locate an external fuel filter on a vehicle with an in-tank integrated filter/pump assembly
Not relieving fuel system pressure before disconnecting fuel lines

stepHints: Most modern vehicles use Electric Power Steering (EPS) which has NO power steering fluid to change
If your steering feels stiff or makes noise, it is likely an EPS motor or sensor issue - not a fluid problem
Consult your owner's manual to confirm whether your vehicle has hydraulic or electric power steering
commonMistakes: Looking for a power steering fluid reservoir on a vehicle with EPS - there is no fluid to check or change
Attempting to add fluid to a system that does not use hydraulic fluid

stepHints: Timing belt replacement is a MAJOR service - typically recommended every 60,000-105,000 miles depending on the engine
This is NOT a DIY job for most owners - it requires significant engine disassembly, specialized tools, and precise timing alignment
IMPORTANT: Many timing belt engines are "interference" designs - if the belt breaks, valves contact pistons causing catastrophic engine damage
When replacing the timing belt, also replace the water pump, tensioner, and idler pulleys (they share the same service life)
Have a qualified mechanic perform this service. Typical cost is $500-1,200 depending on the vehicle
Verify your engine's replacement interval in the owner's manual - do NOT exceed the recommended mileage
specialTools: Professional service strongly recommended
commonMistakes: Exceeding the timing belt replacement interval - a snapped belt on an interference engine destroys the engine
Replacing only the belt and not the water pump/tensioner/idler - these components share the same service life and failing any one of them ruins the new belt
Attempting as a DIY project without proper training - incorrect timing will cause the engine to run poorly or not at all

stepHints: Oil filter is a CARTRIDGE type on TOP of engine - you can access it from above without jacking the car
Open hood, locate plastic oil filter housing cap on top of engine (between coil packs)
Use a 36mm oil filter cap wrench to unscrew the housing cap counter-clockwise
Pull out old cartridge filter element, clean housing interior, install new element
Replace the O-ring on the housing cap - included with quality filter kits (e.g., Mann HU 816 x)
For drain plug access: raise vehicle on jack stands at BMW reinforced jack pads (hard rubber pads on rocker)
17mm drain plug with aluminum crush washer - replace crush washer EVERY oil change, torque to 18 ft-lbs
Fill 5.3 quarts 0W-30 BMW LL-01 approved oil - check iDrive oil level display or dipstick
BMW uses electronic oil level sensor - run engine 2 minutes, wait 5, check via iDrive
specialTools: 36mm oil filter cap wrench (cartridge housing)
17mm socket (drain plug)
BMW crush washer set
commonMistakes: Using non-LL-01 approved oil - standard 'full synthetic' may not meet BMW spec

Reusing aluminum crush washer on drain plug - single use only
Jacking on body seams instead of designated BMW jack pads

stepHints: Disconnect negative battery terminal before starting. Let engine cool completely - spark plug work on a hot engine risks burns and thread damage
Remove engine cover (if equipped) for access to ignition coils
Inline 4-cylinder with 4 plugs in a row along the top of the engine - straightforward access after removing coil packs
Remove ignition coil packs one at a time (typically 8mm or 10mm bolt). Label or photograph if concerned about order
Use spark plug socket (typically 5/8" or 16mm) with extension to remove old plugs. Inspect old plugs for abnormal wear patterns
12 12 0 039 664 (NGK PLKR7B8E) come pre-gapped from factory - do NOT adjust the gap

Install 12 12 0 039 664 (NGK PLKR7B8E) by hand first to avoid cross-threading, then torque to 17 ft-lbs. Do NOT apply anti-seize to modern iridium/platinum plugs - they have factory-applied coating that serves this purpose
Reinstall ignition coils and secure with bolts. Reconnect battery and start engine to verify smooth idle
specialTools: Spark plug socket (5/8" or 16mm, with rubber insert)
Socket extensions (6" and 12")
Torque wrench (inch-lb range)
8mm or 10mm socket (coil pack and engine cover bolts)
commonMistakes: Using wrong spark plug - this vehicle requires 12 12 0 039 664 (NGK PLKR7B8E)
Over-torquing spark plugs (spec is 17 ft-lbs) - overtightening can crack the ceramic or strip aluminum head threads
Applying anti-seize to modern iridium/platinum plugs - they have factory-applied coating, adding more can cause inaccurate torque readings

stepHints: NEVER open a hot cooling system - wait until engine is completely cool. Pressurized coolant can cause severe burns
Locate radiator drain petcock at bottom of radiator (usually driver side). Place drain pan underneath and open to drain old coolant. Capacity is 7.4 qt total system
Once drained, close petcock. Fill system with distilled water, run engine to operating temperature with heater on HIGH, then drain again. Repeat until water runs clear
Refill with BMW Coolant Antifreeze (blue, phosphate-free). BMW/European coolant is phosphate-free - do NOT use conventional US coolant
Bleed air from system: look for bleed valve/screw on thermostat housing or upper radiator hose. Fill slowly, squeeze upper hose to work out air pockets
Run engine to operating temperature with heater on HIGH. Check for leaks at all connections. Recheck coolant level after engine cools and top off
specialTools: Drain pan (capacity for 7.4 qt total system)
Funnel with bleed tube (spill-free type recommended)
Distilled water for flushing
Coolant vacuum fill tool (recommended for European cars with complex routing)
commonMistakes: Using wrong coolant type - this vehicle requires BMW Coolant Antifreeze (blue, phosphate-free)
Mixing different coolant types - can cause gel formation, corrosion, or overheating
Not bleeding air from system - trapped air causes hot spots, overheating, and inaccurate temp gauge readings

stepHints: This vehicle has a sealed transmission (ZF Lifeguard 8 ATF (8HP 8-speed, BMW claims lifetime fill)) - manufacturer states "lifetime fill"
Many independent mechanics recommend fluid service at 60,000-80,000 miles despite "lifetime" claim

stepHints: SAFETY: Brake fluid is corrosive to paint - immediately wipe any spills. Work in a well-ventilated area
This vehicle requires DOT 4 Low Viscosity (BMW spec) brake fluid. Do NOT mix DOT types (especially DOT 5 silicone with DOT 3/4 glycol-based)
Open master cylinder reservoir (under hood, driver side) and top off with fresh DOT 4 Low Viscosity (BMW spec). Keep reservoir topped during bleeding
Bleed brakes starting from the wheel FARTHEST from the master cylinder (typically: RR → LR → RF → LF)

At each wheel: attach clear hose to bleeder valve into catch bottle. Have helper pump brake pedal 3x, hold on last pump. Open bleeder briefly until fluid flows, close, then release pedal. Repeat until no bubbles appear
Wheel removal: use 17mm (note: BMW uses lug BOLTS, not nuts) socket for lug bolts. Torque to 103 ft-lbs when reinstalling
After bleeding all 4 corners: pump brake pedal several times to build pressure. Pedal should feel firm - if spongy, re-bleed
specialTools: Brake bleeder wrench (8mm or 10mm, vehicle-specific)
Clear vinyl hose and catch bottle
Fresh DOT 4 Low Viscosity (BMW spec) brake fluid (1 quart minimum)
Helper for two-person bleed method (or one-person bleeder kit)
17mm (note: BMW uses lug BOLTS, not nuts) socket and breaker bar (wheel removal)
commonMistakes: Using wrong DOT rating - this vehicle requires DOT 4 Low Viscosity (BMW spec)
Letting master cylinder reservoir run dry during bleeding - introduces air into system
Not bleeding in correct order (farthest to nearest from master cylinder)
Using old/opened brake fluid - brake fluid absorbs moisture from air rapidly once opened

stepHints: Loosen lug bolts (17mm (note: BMW uses lug BOLTS, not nuts) socket) while wheel is on ground, then raise vehicle and remove wheel
NOTE: This vehicle uses lug BOLTS (not nuts) - when removing the wheel, the wheel is not held by studs. Use a wheel alignment pin/guide tool to assist with reinstallation
Inspect brake pads through caliper inspection window or by removing caliper. Minimum pad thickness is typically 3mm (1/8") - replace if at or below this
Check brake rotor surface for scoring, grooves, or heat spots (blue discoloration). Measure rotor thickness with micrometer - compare to minimum thickness stamped on rotor
Inspect caliper for leaks, damaged dust boots, and sticky slide pins. Slide pins should move freely
Check brake hoses for cracks, bulging, or leaks
Reinstall wheel and torque lug bolts to 103 ft-lbs in a star/cross pattern. Re-torque after 50-100 miles
specialTools: 17mm (note: BMW uses lug BOLTS, not nuts) socket and breaker bar
Jack and jack stands
Brake pad thickness gauge or micrometer
Flashlight for visual inspection
Wheel alignment guide pins (for lug bolt vehicles)
commonMistakes: Not torquing lug bolts to spec (103 ft-lbs) - under-torque causes wheel loosening, over-torque warps rotors
Ignoring brake fluid level - low fluid often indicates worn pads (fluid fills caliper space as pads wear)
Only checking one corner - brake wear can vary significantly between axles and sides
Trying to hang wheel on studs like American/Japanese cars - lug bolt vehicles require holding the wheel while threading bolts

stepHints: Loosen all lug bolts (17mm (note: BMW uses lug BOLTS, not nuts) socket) while wheels are on ground, then raise vehicle
RWD rotation pattern: Rear tires move straight to front. Front tires cross to opposite rear positions (X-pattern for front tires)
If tires are DIRECTIONAL (arrow on sidewall), they can only be rotated front-to-rear on the same side - never crossed
Check tire pressures and adjust all tires to door placard specification after rotation
Torque all lug bolts to 103 ft-lbs in a star/cross pattern. Re-torque after 50-100 miles of driving
specialTools: 17mm (note: BMW uses lug BOLTS, not nuts) socket and breaker bar
Floor jack and 4 jack stands (or lift)
Torque wrench
Tire pressure gauge
commonMistakes: Not torquing lug bolts to spec (103 ft-lbs)
Rotating directional tires to opposite sides (check for directional arrow on sidewall)
Forgetting to adjust tire pressures after rotation - front and rear specs may differ
Not re-torquing lug nuts/bolts after 50-100 miles

stepHints: Open the hood and locate the air filter box - it is a large plastic housing connected to the intake tube, typically on one side of the engine bay
Release the clips or unscrew the Torx/hex fasteners on the air box lid. European vehicles often use T25 Torx screws instead of simple clips
TURBOCHARGED ENGINE: You may need to disconnect the MAF sensor electrical connector and/or loosen the intake tube clamp before fully removing the air box lid
Lift the lid and remove the old air filter. Note the orientation (airflow direction arrow) for installing the new one
Inspect the air box interior for debris, leaves, or rodent nesting material. Wipe clean if needed
Install the new air filter with the airflow arrow pointing toward the engine (downstream). Ensure it seats flat with no gaps around the edges
Close the air box lid and secure all clips/fasteners. Ensure a tight seal - any air leak bypasses the filter
Reconnect MAF sensor connector and tighten intake tube clamp if disconnected
specialTools: T25 Torx screwdriver (European vehicles often use Torx fasteners on air box)
commonMistakes: Installing filter upside down or backwards - check airflow direction arrow
Not seating filter fully in the air box - gaps allow unfiltered air into engine
Not closing all clips/fasteners on air box lid - causes unmetered air leak and possible check engine light
Forgetting to reconnect MAF sensor connector - causes check engine light and poor running

stepHints: The cabin air filter on this vehicle is accessed from the cowl area (exterior, under the windshield wiper area)
Turn off the ignition and lift the windshield wipers away from the windshield. Remove the cowl panel cover (usually plastic clips or screws)
Locate the cabin filter housing underneath the cowl panel. Open the cover (clips or screws) and slide out the old filter
Note the airflow direction arrow on the old filter before removing. Install new filter with arrow pointing in the same direction (typically downward/into the vehicle)
Reinstall the filter housing cover, cowl panel, and lower windshield wipers
specialTools: Phillips screwdriver or T20 Torx (for cowl panel screws)
Plastic trim removal tool (to avoid breaking cowl panel clips)
commonMistakes: Installing filter with airflow arrow pointing the wrong direction - check arrow before removing old filter
Breaking plastic cowl panel clips during removal - use a trim tool, not a screwdriver, to pry clips
Not replacing cabin filter often enough - a clogged filter reduces HVAC airflow and can cause musty odor

stepHints: Before starting: take a photo of the belt routing or find the belt routing diagram (usually on a sticker in the engine bay or in the owner's manual). This is CRITICAL for reinstallation
European vehicles may use a stretch-fit belt without a traditional tensioner. If your vehicle uses a stretch belt, a special installation tool is required and the belt cannot be reused once removed

Locate the automatic belt tensioner - it is spring-loaded with a smooth (unpainted) idler pulley. Use a 15mm wrench, 3/8" square drive ratchet, or vehicle-specific tensioner tool to rotate the tensioner and release belt tension
Slip the old belt off while holding the tensioner. Inspect all pulleys for smooth spinning and wobble - replace any noisy or rough bearings now while the belt is off
Route the new belt according to the diagram, leaving one pulley for last (usually the tensioner idler or alternator). Rotate tensioner, slip belt onto final pulley, and slowly release tensioner
Verify the belt is properly seated in ALL pulley grooves - a misaligned belt will be thrown off immediately. Start engine briefly to confirm belt tracks correctly
specialTools: Serpentine belt tool or 15mm wrench or 3/8" square drive ratchet (for tensioner)
Flashlight (to inspect belt routing and pulley condition)
Stretch belt installation tool (if applicable to this model)
commonMistakes: Not photographing/documenting belt routing before removal - reinstallation without the diagram is very difficult
Belt not fully seated in a pulley groove - causes squealing, belt damage, or belt being thrown off
Not inspecting idler and tensioner pulleys while belt is off - a failing bearing will destroy the new belt quickly
Releasing tensioner too quickly - let it return slowly to avoid damaging the new belt
Attempting to reuse a stretch-fit belt - these belts are one-time use and must be replaced with new

stepHints: The battery on this vehicle is located in the TRUNK (not under the hood). Look under the trunk floor panel on the right side
NOTE: There may be a remote positive terminal under the hood for jump-starting - this is NOT where the battery is located
SAFETY: Remove any metal jewelry before working on the battery. A wrench bridging positive to ground can cause severe burns or fire
Disconnect the NEGATIVE (-) terminal first (usually 10mm bolt). Move the cable aside so it cannot accidentally contact the terminal
Disconnect the POSITIVE (+) terminal next
Remove the battery hold-down clamp or bracket (typically 10mm, 12mm, or 13mm bolt). Lift the battery out - batteries are heavy (30-50 lbs for cars, 50-75 lbs for trucks)
Clean the battery tray and terminal connectors with baking soda/water solution if there is corrosion. Dry thoroughly
Set new battery in tray and secure hold-down clamp. Connect POSITIVE (+) terminal first, then NEGATIVE (-) last
Apply battery terminal protectant spray or thin layer of dielectric grease to terminals to prevent future corrosion
After connecting: you may need to reset clock, radio presets, and power windows. Some vehicles require an idle relearn procedure - let engine idle for 10 minutes
specialTools: 10mm wrench or socket (terminal bolts)
10mm, 12mm, or 13mm socket (hold-down clamp)
Wire brush or battery terminal cleaner
Memory saver tool (optional - preserves radio, clock, ECU settings during battery swap)
commonMistakes: Disconnecting positive terminal first - always disconnect NEGATIVE first to prevent short circuits
Connecting negative terminal first during installation - always connect POSITIVE first
Not securing hold-down clamp - an unsecured battery can shift and short against the hood
Not cleaning corroded terminals - corrosion on terminals causes voltage drops and starting problems
Looking for the battery under the hood - this vehicle's battery is in the trunk

stepHints: Check your owner's manual or measure your current wiper blades for the correct sizes. Driver and passenger sides are often DIFFERENT lengths
European vehicles often use a specific wiper arm attachment style (pinch tab, push button, or side pin). Verify the connector type before purchasing replacement blades
Lift the wiper arm away from the windshield until it locks in the upright position. Place a folded towel on the windshield under the arm in case it snaps back
Press the release tab on the wiper blade where it connects to the arm. Slide the old blade off the hook (most modern vehicles use a J-hook or push-button adapter)
Attach the new blade by sliding it onto the wiper arm hook until it clicks into place. Gently lower the arm back to the windshield and verify it sits flat
Repeat for the other side. Test both wipers with washer fluid to verify proper sweep and no streaking
specialTools: No tools required - wiper blades are a tool-free replacement on most vehicles
commonMistakes: Buying wrong blade size - driver and passenger sides are usually different lengths
Letting wiper arm snap back against windshield without a blade on it - can crack the glass
Not testing new blades with washer fluid - streaking indicates incorrect installation or defective blade
Buying wrong adapter type - verify J-hook, push-button, pin, or bayonet style before purchasing
